@RoKhanna 
Thanks to Representative Ro Khanna for a thoughtful thread on the direction of technology and automation, particularly the discussion of excessive automation that referenced my work. 
The thread has generated a lot of reactions, and I’d like to add a few thoughts.
Broadly speaking, the comments fall into five categories, and I take each one of these in turn.
1. Is the concept of “excessive automation” even meaningful?
2. Is there really excessive automation?
3. Does the presence of excessive automation somehow call for reversing successful past automation of backbreaking manual tasks and boring office work?
4. Why isn’t the market enough?
5. Do we need an automation tax?
As briefly as I can, my thoughts (based on 15 years of research on this topic) now follow:
1. Using an analogy, sleep is essential. But one can have excessive sleep which interferes with things like productive work. By referring to “excessive automation” the literature means that some amount of automation is good, but it can be in excess of this optimal amount. This means that automation is not bad but there can be too much of it.
2. Yes, I believe there is excessive automation already. We live in the age of innovation. This did not start with AI. Since 1980 the number of patents in the United States has almost quadrupled, and there have been scientific breakthroughs in every field. But aggregate productivity growth (for example, as measured by total factor productivity) has been anemic – much lower than in the three decades or so that followed World War II. Even worse wage growth has been even slower than productivity growth. We are not receiving the benefits of all this innovation, partly because we are not using it correctly. One mistake is that we often double down on automation, and do not use our remarkable technological know-how in other socially beneficial directions – most importantly, for developing more “pro worker” technologies that would make workers more productive and capable of performing more sophisticated and new tasks.
In addition to the aggregate productivity evidence, a lot of recent work (including my papers with Pascual Restrepo) show that rapid automation can create inequality and even wage declines for some types of labor and demographic groups. This suggests that the market may overdo automation, because it is not taking into account its potential negative social consequences.
3. All of this underscores that automation has both good and bad aspects. There may be some marginal types of automation that go beyond what’s socially desirable. Nobody in their right mind would ask society to halt automation, especially AI-based automation. There will be a lot of tasks that will be automated with advances in AI and most of them should be automated.
The problem then is not automation per se. Instead, it is the obsession with automation ahead of everything else, leading to too much automation. As a result, we ignore myriad productive and socially beneficial things that AI can do. Many of these productive activities could be useful to the economy, workers and society. What I call “pro-worker AI” is the key example of this. Pro-worker AI improves the contribution of workers to the production process by providing real-time, context-dependent and relevant information for their problem-solving and task performance.
4. The market is quite efficient in allocating existing goods – be they apples and oranges or T-shirts and pants. But economics also reminds us that that the market does not allocate innovation resources efficiently. This is because innovation creates new knowledge and generates externalities. Moreover, disruptive innovation unleashes a whole series of negative effects on workers, incumbents, and sometimes on groups of consumers.
Put differently, the direction of innovation is easy to distort. This is particularly the case because innovators do not always capture the full gains from new technologies or products, nor do they bear the full burden of disruption.
The balance between automation and creating new tasks for workers is often distorted, not least because it is much harder for innovators to capture the returns that accrue to workers in terms of higher wages. This is all the more so for tech companies.
In addition, most industrialized countries have tax codes that treat capital more favorable than labor. This creates an additional set of forces that push society towards too much automation and not enough pro-worker innovation. For example, in the United States marginal taxes on capital income are near zero and certainly less than 5%, while labor income faces much higher tax rates, often over 30%, including fringe benefits and payroll taxes.
Lack of competition in the tech industry means that it has come to be dominated by a few mega companies. This lack of competition makes it harder to steer technology in a new direction. These mega companies have business models that depend on either automation or digital ad revenue. New direction should come from new entrants and startups. However, small companies in Silicon Valley are today either crushed or acquired by Big Tech.
In sum, there are reasons to suspect that left to its own devices, the market will not deliver a sufficient amount of pro-worker AI. This leads to too much automation using advances in AI. This is analogous to the market needing policy interventions to kickstart the energy transition and investments in renewables.
5. All of this says that if we managed to redirect technological change in a more pro-worker direction, society would benefit.
This analysis does not necessarily call for robot or automation taxes, however. Getting rid of existing distortions that favor automation and introducing subsidies and additional funding opportunities for new pro-worker technologies would be the better way to go. It is true, developing a reliable measurement framework for worker technologies takes work, and it will never be perfect. We will always have a situation where some automation technologies will get mislabeled as pro-worker and received subsidies. But we should not shy away from automation. More importantly, we should counterbalance it with other technological advances, especially pro-worker AI.

But America is not facing an ordinary moment. We have levels of wealth concentration not seen since the first Gilded Age. Millions of young people cannot afford a home, childcare, healthcare, or college. Voting rights and women’s rights are being rolled back. Black and Latino communities, rural America, and factory towns have been excluded from the wealth generation of the modern economy.

The answer to a crisis of this scale is not caution. It is a bold vision equal to the moment.

We cannot simply be against Trumpism and go back to a status quo that tore this nation apart. We need a new economic patriotism that creates good jobs in every ZIP code, rebuilds American industry, delivers Medicare for All, provides childcare $10 day, makes public college tuition-free, creates 1,000 new trade schools and technical institutes, guarantees homeownership for every American who works hard by age 35, and ensures that the gains from AI and technological progress are shared by working and middle-class Americans.
